text: Why does the JVM need a separate `invokeinterface` instruction rather than using `invokevirtual`?
choices: Interfaces are loaded lazily, so their methods do not exist when `invokevirtual` would be resolved.
Interface methods are always public, and `invokevirtual` cannot express public dispatch.
A class may implement any combination of interfaces, so no single method-table layout can give an interface method a fixed slot.
Interface methods may have default bodies, which `invokevirtual` has no way to locate.
explanation: For classes, a subclass keeps the superclass's table layout, so a slot number computed at compile time stays valid forever. Interfaces break that: if `Dot` implements both `Drawable` and `Comparable2`, both cannot claim slot 0, and there is no layout that works for every possible combination. So the lookup must search rather than index. Call-site caching brings the measured cost back down to roughly that of a virtual call.
